summary: TalkSport explains where the Manchester United takeover stands after Qatari Sheikh Jassim bin Al Thani withdrew, leaving Sir Jim Ratcliffe with an agreement in principle to buy a 25 per cent stake for £1.3billion. It traces the saga from the Glazers' November 2022 announcement, covers the board meeting, the Premier League owners and directors test, and Ratcliffe's plans for football operations and Old Trafford. Fans are unhappy the Glazers will remain, though this is seen as a first step toward Ratcliffe taking full control.
one_line: Sir Jim Ratcliffe nears a £1.3bn deal for a 25% Manchester United stake after Sheikh Jassim withdrew, with board approval and league checks still ahead.
key_facts: Sir Jim Ratcliffe has an offer of £1.3billion for a 25 per cent stake in Manchester United, the club he has supported since childhood.
The Glazers announced in November 2022, during the Qatar World Cup, that they were open to offers for all or some of their shares in United.
The Glazer regime began with a leveraged buyout in 2005 that saddled United with debts that at one stage soared to as high as £1bn.
Joel and Avram Glazer, the two most hands-on of the six Glazer siblings, hired the New York-based Raine banking group to run the bidding process.
Raine had brokered Todd Boehly's £4.5bn commitment to take control of Chelsea, giving the Glazers hopes of getting as much as double for United.
The race came down to Oldham-born Ratcliffe, who had previously offered £4bn for Chelsea, and Qatari Sheikh Jassim bin Al Thani, who set up the '92 Foundation'.
Sheikh Jassim withdrew from the bidding at the end of the week before the article, leaving the way clear for Ratcliffe.
Half of United's 12-strong board are Glazer family members, and Joel and Avram as co-chairmen have the deciding say in a split vote.
It is far from guaranteed Ratcliffe's proposal will be put to a vote at Thursday's pre-arranged board meeting, as several details remain to be settled.
Ratcliffe is likely to need at least a couple of months to pass the Premier League's owners and directors test, made more stringent after Portsmouth went into administration in 2010.
Ratcliffe wants an executive role, control of day-to-day football matters and his own sporting director, with Paul Mitchell one of the main names in the frame.
Ratcliffe plans to upgrade Old Trafford into a 90,000-seat stadium and wants the deal ratified for the January transfer window, though FFP concerns may limit spending.
Ratcliffe already owns Nice in France and Lausanne in Switzerland, and turns 71 a day before the board meeting.
